questions.q: How were the indigenous peoples of North America displaced by European settlers?
answer: The native peoples of North America, who had lived there for thousands of years, were displaced by waves of European settlers.

answer.text: European contact brought diseases such as smallpox, to which the natives had no immunity. These epidemics killed enormous numbers, far more than were lost in warfare, weakening whole communities.

Settlers regarded land as private property to be owned, farmed and sold, an idea foreign to the natives, who lived in harmony with nature. As the frontier moved westward through purchase, war and broken treaties, natives were pushed off their ancestral lands.
Eventually the surviving natives were confined to reservations, often poor land, while the buffalo they depended on were destroyed, ruining their way of life.

answer: Thus disease, land hunger and force together dispossessed the indigenous peoples of America.

questions.q: Describe the impact of European settlement on the Aborigines of Australia.
answer: The coming of Europeans had a devastating impact on the Aborigines, the original inhabitants of Australia.

answer.text: From 1788 the British used Australia as a penal colony, sending convicts there. Free settlers followed, and they steadily took over land for farming and grazing.

The Aborigines, who had lived on the continent for tens of thousands of years, were driven off their lands. Their numbers fell sharply due to disease, violence and loss of livelihood. The doctrine of terra nullius, that the land belonged to no one, was used to deny their rights to it.
Only in the twentieth century did movements grow to recognise Aboriginal rights, restore land claims, and offer apologies for past injustices.

answer: European settlement thus brought near destruction, followed by a slow recovery of rights.

questions.q: How did the discovery of gold and the growth of railways transform the settler economies?

answer.text: rapidly transformed the settler economies of North America and Australia.

list: Gold rushes drew huge numbers of hopeful migrants, swelling the population almost overnight
New towns, trade and industry sprang up around the mining regions
Railways carried people and goods across vast distances, linking coasts and interiors
They made distant farms and mines profitable and sped the settlement of the land, though at the further expense of native peoples
